questions.q: In a group of $400$ people, $160$ are smokers and non-vegetarian; $100$ are smokers and vegetarian and the remaining $140$ are non-smokers and vegetarian. Their chances of getting a particular chest disorder are $35 % , 20 %$ and $10 %$ respectively. A person is chosen from the group at random and is found to be suffering from the chest disorder. The probability that the selected person is a smoker and non-vegetarian is :
questions.solution:
Consider following events
$A$ : Person chosen is a smoker and non
vegetarian.

$B$ : Person chosen is a smoker and vegetarian.

$C$ : Person chosen is a non-smoker and vegetarian

$E$ : Person chosen has a chest disorder

Given

$P\left(A\right) = \dfrac{160}{400}P\left(B\right) = \dfrac{100}{400}P\left(C\right) = \dfrac{140}{400}$

$P\left(\dfrac{E}{A}\right) = \dfrac{35}{100}P\left(\dfrac{E}{B}\right) = \dfrac{20}{100}P\left(\dfrac{E}{C}\right) = \dfrac{10}{100}$

To find

$P\left(\dfrac{A}{E}\right) = \dfrac{P\left(A\right)P\left(\dfrac{E}{A}\right)}{P\left(A\right) \cdot P\left(\dfrac{E}{A}\right) + P\left(B\right) \cdot P\left(\dfrac{E}{B}\right) + P\left(C\right) \cdot P\left(\dfrac{E}{C}\right)}$

$= \dfrac{\dfrac{160}{400} \times \dfrac{35}{100}}{\dfrac{160}{400} \times \dfrac{35}{100} + \dfrac{100}{400} \times \dfrac{20}{100} + \dfrac{140}{400} \times \dfrac{10}{100}}$

$= \dfrac{28}{45}$

option $\left(4\right)$

questions.q: Let $A$ be a set of all $4$ -digit natural numbers whose exactly one digit is $7$. Then the probability that a randomly chosen element of $A$ leaves remainder $2$ when divided by $5$ is:
questions.solution:
$n\left(s\right) = n$( when $7$ appears on thousands place ) $+ n$($7$ does not appear on thousands place)

$= 9 \times 9 \times 9 + 8 \times 9 \times 9 \times 3$

$= 33 \times 9 \times 9$

$n\left(E\right) = n$( last digit $7 \text{ and } 7$ appears once)$+ n$( last digit $2$ when $7$ appears once)

$= 8 \times 9 \times 9 + \left(9 \times 9 + 8 \times 9 \times 2\right)$

$∴ P\left(E\right) = \dfrac{8 \times 9 \times 9 + 9 \times 25}{33 \times 9 \times 9} = \dfrac{97}{297}$

questions.q: Let ${B}_{i}\left(i = 1, 2, 3\right)$ be three independent events in a sample space. The probability that only ${B}_{1}$ occur is $\alpha,$ only ${B}_{2}$ occurs is $\beta$ and only ${B}_{3}$ occurs is $\gamma .$ Let $p$ be the probability that none of the events ${B}_{i}$ occurs and these $4$ probabilities satisfy the equations $\left(\alpha - 2\beta\right)p = \alpha\beta$ and $\left(\beta - 3\gamma\right)p = 2\beta\gamma$ (All the probabilities are assumed to lie in the interval $\left\left(0, 1\right)\right)$ Then $\dfrac{P\left({B}_{1}\right)}{P\left({B}_{3}\right)}$ is equal to______.
questions.solution:
Let $P\left({B}_{1}\right) = {p}_{1}, P\left({B}_{2}\right) = {p}_{2}, P\left({B}_{3}\right) = {p}_{3}$

given that ${p}_{1}\left(1 - {p}_{2}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{3}\right) = \alpha \ldots \left(i\right)$

${p}_{2}\left(1 - {p}_{1}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{3}\right) = \beta \ldots \left(ii\right)$

${p}_{3}\left(1 - {p}_{1}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{2}\right) = \gamma \ldots \left(iii\right)$

and $\left(1 - {p}_{1}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{2}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{3}\right) = p \ldots \left(iv\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{{p}_{1}}{1 - {p}_{1}} = \dfrac{\alpha}{p}, \dfrac{{p}_{2}}{1 - {p}_{2}} = \dfrac{\beta}{p}$ and $\dfrac{{p}_{3}}{1 - {p}_{3}} = \dfrac{\gamma}{p}$

Also $\beta = \dfrac{\alphap}{\alpha + 2p} = \dfrac{3\gammap}{p - 2\gamma}$

$⇒ \alphap - 2\alpha\gamma = 3\alpha\gamma + 6p\gamma$

$⇒ \alphap - 6p\gamma = 5\alpha\gamma$

$⇒ \dfrac{{p}_{1}}{1 - {p}_{1}} - \dfrac{6{p}_{3}}{1 - {p}_{3}} = \dfrac{5{p}_{1}{p}_{3}}{\left(1 - {p}_{1}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{3}\right)}$

$⇒ {p}_{1} - 6{p}_{3} = 0$

$⇒ \dfrac{{p}_{1}}{{p}_{3}} = 6$

The probability that only ${B}_{1}$ occur is $\alpha,$ only ${B}_{2}$ occurs is $\beta$ and only ${B}_{3}$ occurs is $\gamma .$ Let $p$ be the probability that none of the events ${B}_{i}$ occurs and these $4$ probabilities satisfy the equations $\left(\alpha - 2\beta\right)p = \alpha\beta$ and $\left(\beta - 3\gamma\right)p = 2\beta\gamma$ (All the probabilities are assumed to lie in the interval $\left\left(0, 1\right)\right)$ Then $\dfrac{P\left({B}_{1}\right)}{P\left({B}_{3}\right)}$ is equal to______.
questions.explanation:
Let $P\left({B}_{1}\right) = {p}_{1}, P\left({B}_{2}\right) = {p}_{2}, P\left({B}_{3}\right) = {p}_{3}$

given that ${p}_{1}\left(1 - {p}_{2}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{3}\right) = \alpha \ldots \left(i\right)$

${p}_{2}\left(1 - {p}_{1}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{3}\right) = \beta \ldots \left(ii\right)$

${p}_{3}\left(1 - {p}_{1}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{2}\right) = \gamma \ldots \left(iii\right)$

and $\left(1 - {p}_{1}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{2}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{3}\right) = p \ldots \left(iv\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{{p}_{1}}{1 - {p}_{1}} = \dfrac{\alpha}{p}, \dfrac{{p}_{2}}{1 - {p}_{2}} = \dfrac{\beta}{p}$ and $\dfrac{{p}_{3}}{1 - {p}_{3}} = \dfrac{\gamma}{p}$

Also $\beta = \dfrac{\alphap}{\alpha + 2p} = \dfrac{3\gammap}{p - 2\gamma}$

$⇒ \alphap - 2\alpha\gamma = 3\alpha\gamma + 6p\gamma$

$⇒ \alphap - 6p\gamma = 5\alpha\gamma$

$⇒ \dfrac{{p}_{1}}{1 - {p}_{1}} - \dfrac{6{p}_{3}}{1 - {p}_{3}} = \dfrac{5{p}_{1}{p}_{3}}{\left(1 - {p}_{1}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{3}\right)}$

$⇒ {p}_{1} - 6{p}_{3} = 0$

$⇒ \dfrac{{p}_{1}}{{p}_{3}} = 6$

questions.q: Out of 11 consecutive natural number if three numbers are selected at random (without repetition), then the probability that they are in A.P. with positive common difference is :
questions.solution:
$2b = a + c ⇒$sum of $a\text{\text{ and }}c$ is even and $b$ depends on $a\text{\text{ and }}c$

Thus, we can not choose all three independently, but we can choose $a\text{\text{ and }}c$

Moreover, $a\text{and}c$ should be both either even or odd as their sum is even.

Out of $11$ consecutive natural numbers, either five are even and six are odd or six are even and five are odd.

Hence, $P = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{C2 5 + C2 6}{C3 11} + \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{C2 6 + C2 5}{C3 11} = \dfrac{5}{33}$

questions.q: Four fair dice are thrown independently 27 times. Then the expected number of times, at least two dice show up a three or a five, is
questions.solution:
There are only two outcomes, success which stands for getting either 3 or 5, and failure, stands for getting any other outcome.

Probability for success$= p = \dfrac{2}{6}$

Probability for failure$= q = \dfrac{4}{6}$

Number of trials$= n = 27$

Number of dice$= 4$

Using Binomial Probability,

P(at least 2 shows 3 or 5) $= C2 4 \cdot {\left(\dfrac{2}{6}\right)}^{2}{\left(\dfrac{4}{6}\right)}^{2} + C3 4 {\left(\dfrac{2}{6}\right)}^{3}\left(\dfrac{4}{6}\right) + C4 4 {\left(\dfrac{2}{6}\right)}^{4}$

$= \dfrac{384 + 128 + 16}{{6}^{4}} = \dfrac{11}{27}$

Expectation is numerically same as mean.

$∴$ expectation$= np$

$= 27 \cdot \dfrac{11}{27} = 11$

questions.q: In a game two players $A$ and $B$ take turns in throwing a pair of fair dice starting with player $A$ and total of scores on the two dice, in each throw is noted. $A$ wins the game if he throws a total of $6$ before $B$ throws a total of $7$ and $B$ wins the game if he throws a total of $7$ before $A$ throws a total of six. The game stops as soon as either of the players wins. The probability of $A$ winning the game is :
questions.solution:
Sum $6 \to ( 1, 5 ) , ( 5, 1 ) , ( 3, 3 ) , ( 2, 4 ) , ( 4, 2 )$
Sum $7 \to ( 1, 6 ) , ( 6, 1 ) , ( 5, 2 ) , ( 2, 5 ) , ( 3, 4 ) , ( 4, 3 )$

$P ( A\text{wins} ) = P ( A ) + P ( \overset{¯}{A} ) \cdot P ( \overset{¯}{B} ) \cdot P ( A ) + P ( \overset{¯}{A} ) P ( \overset{¯}{B} ) \cdot P ( \overset{¯}{A} ) \cdot P ( \overset{¯}{B} ) \cdot P ( A ) + \ldots \ldots$

We see that this is an infinite G.P. with common ratio $P ( \overset{¯}{A} ) \times P ( \overset{¯}{B} )$

Thus, probability that $A$ wins $= \dfrac{P ( A )}{1 - P ( \overset{¯}{A} ) P ( \overset{¯}{B} )}$
$= \dfrac{\dfrac{5}{36}}{1 - \dfrac{31}{36} \cdot \dfrac{30}{36}} = \dfrac{30}{61}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The probability that a randomly chosen $5$- digit number is made from exactly two digits is :
questions.solution:
Total number of five-digit numbers are $9\left({10}^{4}\right)$.

Case I : Choosing two non-zero digits i.e. in $C2 9$ ways.

So, number of five-digit numbers containing both digits $= {2}^{5} - 2$.

Case II : Choose one non-zero and one zero as digit i.e. in $C1 9$ ways.

So, number of five-digit numbers containing one non-zero and one zero both $= {2}^{4} - 1$.

So, favourable number of ways $= C2 9 \left({2}^{5} - 2\right) + C1 9 \left({2}^{4} - 1\right) = 36\left(30\right) + 9\left(15\right) = 1080 + 135 = 1215$

Thus, required probability $= \dfrac{1215}{9 \times {10}^{4}} = \dfrac{135}{{10}^{4}}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: A die is thrown two times and the sum of the scores appearing on the die is observed to be a multiple of $4$. Then the conditional probability that the score $4$ has appeared at least once is
questions.solution:
A die is thrown two times.

Total number of possible outcomes$= 36$.

Let $E$ is the event that sum of the score appearing on the die is multiple of $4$.

Possible outcomes in favor of $E = \left\{\left(1, 3\right), \left(3, 1\right), \left(2, 2\right), \left(2, 6\right), \left(6, 2\right), \left(3, 5\right), \left(5, 3\right), \left(4, 4\right), \left(6, 6\right)\right\}$.

Number of favorable outcomes$= 9$.

$P\left(E\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

Let $F$ is the event that at least one $4$ appear.

Possible outcomes in favor of $F = \left\{\left(1, 4\right), \left(4, 1\right), \left(2, 4\right), \left(4, 2\right), \left(3, 4\right), \left(4, 3\right), \left(4, 4\right), \left(4, 5\right), \left(5, 4\right), \left(4, 6\right), \left(6, 4\right)\right\}$

$E ∩ F = \left\{\left(4, 4\right)\right\}$

$⇒ P\left(E ∩ F\right) = \dfrac{1}{36}$.

We have to find conditional probability of occurrence of at least one $4$ given that sum of scores is multiple of $4$.

$P\left(F / E\right) = \dfrac{P\left(E ∩ F\right)}{P\left(E\right)} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{36}}{\dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{9}$.

questions.q: Minimum number of times a fair coin must be tossed so that the probability of getting at least one head is more than $99%$ is:
questions.solution:
Let coin is tossed $n$ times.

The probability of getting a head in a single throw of a die is $\dfrac{1}{2} .$

By using binomial theorem, we know that the probability that an event $X$ appear $r$ times in $n$ trials is $P\left(X = r\right) = Cr n {p}^{n - r}{q}^{r}, q = 1 - p, r = 0, 1, 2, . . . , n .$

Now, $P ($at least are head$) = 1 - P ($no head$)$

$= 1 - {\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{n}$

Using, the given condition, we get

$1 - {\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{n} \ge 0.99$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{n} \le 1 - 0.99$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{n} \le \dfrac{1}{100}$

As, ${2}^{6} = 64$ and ${2}^{7} = 128,$ hence, the minimum value of $n$ is $7 .$

questions.q: Two newspapers $A$ and $B$ are published in a city. It is known that $25 %$ of the city population reads $A$ and $20 %$ reads $B$ while $8 %$ reads both $A$ and $B .$ Further, $30 %$ of those who read $A$ but not $B$ look into advertisements and $40 %$ of those who read $B$ but not $A$ also look into advertisements, while $50 %$ of those who read both $A$ and $B$ look into advertisements. Then the percentage of the population who look into advertisements is:
questions.solution:
Let $n\left(A\right)$ and $n\left(B\right)$ be the percentage of population in a city who read newspaper $A$ and $B$ respectively.

Therefore, $n\left(A\right) = 25,$n\left(B\right) = 20$ and $n\left(A ∩ B\right) = 8$

Now, we know that

$n\left(A ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) = n\left(A\right) - n\left(A ∩ B\right)$

$⇒ n\left(A ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) = 25 - 8$

$⇒ n\left(A ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) = 17$

And,

$n\left(\overset{¯}{A} ∩ B\right) = n\left(B\right) - n\left(A ∩ B\right)$

$⇒ n\left(\overset{¯}{A} ∩ B\right) = 20 - 8$

$⇒ n\left(\overset{¯}{A} ∩ B\right) = 12$

Therefore, percentage of those who read advertisements is

$= 30 %$ of $n\left(A ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) + 40 %$ of $n\left(B ∩ \overset{¯}{A}\right) + 50 %$ of $n\left(A ∩ B\right)$

$= \dfrac{30}{100} \times 17 + \dfrac{40}{100} \times 12 + \dfrac{50}{100} \times 8$

$= \dfrac{1390}{100}$

Total persons who look into advertisement $= 13.9%$

questions.q: Four persons can hit a target correctly with probabilities $\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{1}{4}$ and $\dfrac{1}{8}$ respectively. If all hit at the target independently, then the probability that the target would be hit, is
questions.solution:
$P ($target is hit$) = 1 – P ($no one hit the target$)$

$= 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) \cdot \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4}\right) \cdot \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) \cdot \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{8}\right)$

$= 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{3}{4} \cdot \dfrac{2}{3} \cdot \dfrac{7}{8}$

$= 1 - \dfrac{7}{32} = \dfrac{25}{32} .$

Thus, the required probability is $\dfrac{25}{32} .$

Lets draw the venn diagram according to question,

$P\left(\dfrac{A}{B}\right) = \dfrac{P ( A ∩ B )}{P ( B )} = \dfrac{P ( A )}{P ( B )} [ A ⊂ B ⇒ A ∩ B = A ]$

Now, since $P ( B ) \le 1$

$⇒ P\left(\dfrac{A}{B}\right) = \dfrac{P\left(A\right)}{P\left(B\right)} \ge P\left(A\right)$

$⇒ P\left(A | B\right) \ge P ( A )$

questions.q: In a class of $60$ students, $40$ opted for NCC, $30$ opted for NSS and $20$ opted for both NCC and NSS. If one of these students is selected at random, then the probability that the student selected has opted neither for NCC nor for NSS is :
questions.solution:
Let $A \text{ and } B$ be the sets for NCC and NSS respectively.

Given $n\left(A\right) = 40, n\left(B\right) = 30, n\left(A ∩ B\right) = 20$

$∴ n\left(A ∪ B\right) = n\left(A\right) + n\left(B\right) - n\left(A ∩ B\right)$

$= 40 + 30 - 20 = 50$

$∴ P\left(A ∪ B\right) = \dfrac{50}{60} = \dfrac{5}{6}$

$∴ P{\left(A ∪ B\right)}^{′} = 1 - P\left(A ∪ B\right)$

$= 1 - \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{1}{6}$

questions.q: In a game, a man wins Rs. $100$ if he gets $5$ or $6$ on a throw of a fair die and loses Rs. $50$ for getting any other number on the die. If he decides to throw the die either till he gets a five or a six or to a maximum of three throws, then his expected gain/loss (in rupees) is :
questions.solution:
Probability of success i.e. getting a $5$ or $6 = P\left(s\right) = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

So, probability of failure i.e. getting any number other than $5$ or $6 = P\left(f\right) = 1 - P\left(s\right) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

Let $X$ be the amount that a man wins in a maximum of three throws.

So, $X$ can take values :

Case I : First two throws are $5$ or $6$, game stops

$⇒ X = 100 ⇒ P\left(X = 100\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Case II : First throw is other than $5$ or $6$ and second and third throws are $5$ or $6$, game stops

$⇒ X = 50 ⇒ P\left(X = 50\right) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2}{9}$

Case III : First two throws are other than $5$ or $6$ and last throw is $5$ or $6$

$⇒ X = 0 ⇒ P\left(X = 0\right) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{4}{27}$

Case IV : All three throws are other than $5$ or $6$

$⇒ X = - 150 ⇒ P\left(X = - 150\right) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{8}{27}$

Therefore, expected gain or loss

$= E\left(X\right) = 100 \times \dfrac{1}{3} + 50 \times \dfrac{2}{9} + 0 \times \dfrac{4}{27} - 150 \times \dfrac{8}{27} = 0$

questions.q: In a random experiment, a fair die is rolled until two fours are obtained in succession. The probability that the experiment will end in the fifth throw of the die is equal to :
questions.solution:
The probability of getting a $4$ in a throw of a die is $\dfrac{1}{6}$.

The probability of getting other than $4$ i.e. $4$ i.e. numbers $1, 2, 3, 5 \text{ and } 6$ in a single throw of a die is $\dfrac{5}{6}$.

Total throws done $= 5$.

For the event to be completed in ${5}^{th}$ throw, ${4}^{th}$ and ${5}^{th}$ throw must be $4$ . Also, ${3}^{rd}$ throw must be other than $4$ i.e. $4$. Hence, cases for the first two position can be :

Case I : ${1}^{st}$ throw must be $4$ and ${2}^{nd}$ throw must not be $4$ i.e. $4$

Thus, $P\left(4\overset{-}{4}\overset{-}{4}44\right) = \dfrac{1}{6} . \dfrac{5}{6} . \dfrac{5}{6} . \dfrac{1}{6} . \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{25}{{6}^{5}}$.

Case II : ${1}^{st}$ throw must not be $4$ i.e. $4$ and ${2}^{nd}$ throw must not be $4$ i.e. $4$

Thus, $P\left(\overset{-}{4}\overset{-}{4}\overset{-}{4}44\right) = \dfrac{5}{6} . \dfrac{5}{6} . \dfrac{5}{6} . \dfrac{1}{6} . \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{125}{{6}^{5}}$.

Case III : ${1}^{st}$ throw must not be $4$ i.e. $4$ and ${2}^{nd}$ throw must be $4$

Thus, $P\left(\overset{-}{4}4\overset{-}{4}44\right) = \dfrac{5}{6} . \dfrac{1}{6} . \dfrac{5}{6} . \dfrac{1}{6} . \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{25}{{6}^{5}}$.

Therefore, probability that experiment will end in the fifth throw given that two fours occurred in succession will be

$P\left(4\overset{-}{4}\overset{-}{4}44\right) + P\left(\overset{-}{4}4\overset{-}{4}44\right) + P\left(\overset{-}{4}\overset{-}{4}\overset{-}{4}44\right)$

$= \dfrac{25}{{6}^{5}} + \dfrac{25}{{6}^{5}} + \dfrac{125}{{6}^{5}}$

$= \dfrac{175}{{6}^{5}}$.

questions.q: Let $\mathrm{S}=\{1,2, \ldots . ., 20\}$. A subset $\mathrm{B}$ of $\mathrm{S}$ is said to be "nice", if the sum of the elements of $\mathrm{B}$ is 203 . Than the probability that a randomly chosen subset of $S$ is "nice" is :
questions.solution:
Since total number of subsets of the set $S=2^{20}$

Now, the sum of all number from 1 to $20=\frac{20 \times 21}{2}=210$ Then, find the sets which has sum 7 .

(1) $\{7\}$

(2) $\{1,6\}$

(3) $\{2,5\}$

(4) $\{3,4\}$

(5) $\{1,2,4\}$

Then, there is only 5 sets which has sum 203

Hence required probability $=\frac{5}{2^{20}}$

questions.q:
A bag contains 30 white balls and 10 red balls. 16 balls are drawn one by one randomly from the bag with replacement. If $X$ be the number of white balls drawn, then

$\left(\frac{\text{ mean of } \mathrm{X}}{\text{ standard deviation of } \mathrm{X}}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: $P($ white ball $)=\frac{30}{40}=\frac{3}{4}, Q$ (red ball) $=\frac{10}{40}=\frac{1}{4}, n=16 \frac{\text{ Mean of } X}{\text{ standard deviation of } X}=\frac{n P}{\sqrt{n P Q}}=\frac{\sqrt{n P}}{\sqrt{Q}} =\sqrt{\frac{16 \times \frac{3}{4}}{\frac{1}{4}}}=\sqrt{48}=4 \sqrt{3}$

questions.q: Two integers are selected at random from the set $\{1,2, \ldots, 11\}$. Given that the sum of selected numbers is even, the conditional probability that both the numbers are even is :
questions.solution:
Probability of getting sum of selected two numbers is even

$=P\left(E_{1}\right)=\frac{{ }^{5} C_{2}+{ }^{5} C_{2}}{{ }^{11} C_{2}}$

Probability of getting sum is even and selected numbers are also even $P\left(E_{2}\right)=\frac{{ }^{5} C_{2}}{{ }^{11} C_{2}}$

Hence, $P\left(\frac{E_{2}}{E_{1}}\right)=\frac{{ }^{5} C_{2}}{{ }^{6} C_{2}+{ }^{5} C_{2}}=\frac{10}{15+10}=\frac{2}{5}$.

questions.q: If the probability of hitting a target by a shooter, in any shot is $\dfrac{1}{3},$ then the minimum number of independent shots at the target required by him so that the probability of hitting the target at least once is greater than $\dfrac{5}{6},$ is:
questions.solution:
$P\left(hittingtarget\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Let number of trials $= n$

$P\left(hittingtargetatleastonce\right)$

$= 1 - P$\left(nothit\right)$

$= 1 - {\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}^{n} > \dfrac{5}{6}$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right) > {\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}^{n}$

So minimum number of trials $= 5$

questions.q: An unbiased coin is tossed. If the outcome is a head then a pair of unbiased dice is rolled and the sum of the numbers obtained on them is noted. If the toss of the coin results in tail then a card from a well-shuffled pack of nine cards numbered $1,2, 3, \ldots , 9$ is randomly picked and the number on the card is noted. The probability that the noted number is either $7$ or $8$ is
questions.solution:
Let, A$ be the event that the noted number is either $7 or 8 .

And, ${E}_{1}$ be the event that the toss of coin results in head and ${E}_{2}$ be the event that the toss of coin results in tail.

Then, we have $P\left({E}_{1}\right) = P \left({E}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

And, $P\left(A | {E}_{1}\right) =P ($getting the sum of the numbers on the pair of dice as $7 or 8 )$

The total number of cases, when a pair of dice is thrown are $= 6 \times 6 = 36$ and the cases of getting sum $7 or 8$ are $\left\{\left(1, 6\right), \left(2, 5\right), \left(3, 4\right), \left(4, 3\right), \left(5, 2\right), \left(6, 1\right), \left(2, 6\right), \left(3, 5\right), \left(4, 4\right), \left(5, 3\right), \left(6, 2\right)\right\} = 11$ cases.

$⇒ P \left(A | {E}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{11}{36}$

Similarly, $P\left(A | {E}_{2}\right) = ($getting the number $7 or 8$ from the numbers $1, 2, 3, . . , 9 )$

$⇒ P \left(A | {E}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{2}{9}$

Now, using the $total probability theorem, we get

P\left(A\right) = P \left({E}_{1}\right)P\left(A | {E}_{1}\right) + P \left({E}_{1}\right)P\left(A | {E}_{2}\right)

$⇒ P$\left(A\right)$ = $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{11}{36} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{2}{9}$

$⇒ P\left(A\right) = \dfrac{11}{72} + \dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{19}{72}$ .

questions.q: An urn contains $5$ red and $2$ green balls. A ball is drawn at random from the urn. If the drawn ball is green, then a red ball is added to the urn and if the drawn ball is red, then a green ball is added to the urn; the original ball is not returned to the urn. Now, a second ball is drawn at random from it. The probability that the second ball is red, is:
questions.solution:
Let $A$ is event that $2nd$ drawn ball is red.

$∴ P\left(A\right) = P\left(R\right) \times P\left(A / R\right) + P\left(G\right) \times P\left(A / G\right)$

$= \dfrac{5}{7} \times \dfrac{4}{7} + \dfrac{2}{7} \times \dfrac{6}{7}$

$= \dfrac{32}{49}$

questions.q: Two cards are drawn successively with replacement from a well-shuffled deck of $52$ cards. Let $X$ denote the random variable of number of aces obtained in the two drawn cards. Then $P\left(X = 1\right) + P\left(X = 2\right)$ equals:
questions.solution:
Using the concept of complementary events,

$P\left(x = 1\right) + P\left(x = 2\right) = 1 - P\left(x = 0\right)$

$= 1 - \dfrac{48}{52} \times \dfrac{48}{52}$

$= 1 - \dfrac{144}{169} = \dfrac{25}{169}$

questions.q: Two different families $A$ and $B$ are blessed with equal number of children. There are $3$ tickets to be distributed amongst the children of these families so that no child gets more than one ticket. If the probability that all the tickets go to the children of the family $B$ is $\dfrac{1}{12},$ then the number of children in each family is
questions.solution:
Let $n$ number of children be there in each family.

$\dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{{}^{n}{C}_{3} \cdot 3 !}{{}^{2n}{C}_{3} \cdot 3 !}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{}^{n}{C}_{3}}{{}^{2n}{C}_{3}} = \dfrac{1}{12}$

$⇒ \dfrac{n\left(n - 1\right)\left(n - 2\right)}{2n\left(2n - 1\right)\left(2n - 2\right)} = \dfrac{1}{12}$

$⇒ \dfrac{n - 2}{2n - 1} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ 3n - 6 = 2n - 1$

$⇒ n = 5$

questions.q: Let $A, B$ and $C$ be three events, which are pair-wise independent and $\overset{¯}{E}$ denotes the complement of an event $E$. If $P\left(A ∩ B ∩ C\right) = 0$ and $P\left(C\right) > 0,$ then $P\left[\left(\overset{¯}{A} ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) | C\right]$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$P\left[\left(\overset{¯}{A} ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) | C\right] = \dfrac{P\left[\left(\overset{¯}{A} ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) ∩ C\right]}{P\left(C\right)}$

$= \dfrac{P\left(C\right) - P\left(A ∩ C\right) - P\left(B ∩ C\right) + P\left(A ∩ B ∩ C\right)}{P\left(C\right)}$

$= \dfrac{P\left(C\right) - P\left(A\right)P\left(C\right) - P\left(B\right)P\left(C\right)}{P\left(C\right)}$

$= 1 - P\left(A\right) - P\left(B\right)$

$= P\left(\overset{¯}{A}\right) - P\left(B\right)$ or $P\left(\overset{¯}{B}\right) - P\left(A\right)$

questions.explanation:
$P\left[\left(\overset{¯}{A} ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) | C\right] = \dfrac{P\left[\left(\overset{¯}{A} ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) ∩ C\right]}{P\left(C\right)}$

$= \dfrac{P\left(C\right) - P\left(A ∩ C\right) - P\left(B ∩ C\right) + P\left(A ∩ B ∩ C\right)}{P\left(C\right)}$

$= \dfrac{P\left(C\right) - P\left(A\right)P\left(C\right) - P\left(B\right)P\left(C\right)}{P\left(C\right)}$

$= 1 - P\left(A\right) - P\left(B\right)$

$= P\left(\overset{¯}{A}\right) - P\left(B\right)$ or $P\left(\overset{¯}{B}\right) - P\left(A\right)$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: A player $X$ has a biased coin whose probability of showing heads is $p$ and a player $Y$ has a fair coin. They start playing a game with their own coins and play alternately. The player who throws a head first is a winner. If $X$ starts the game, and the probability of winning the game by both the players is equal, then the value of ' $p$ ' is
questions.solution:
If the outcome is one of the following: $H, T T H, T T T T H, \ldots$, then $X$ wins As subsequent tosses are independent, so the probability that $X$ wins is

p+$\frac{p}{4}+\frac{p}{16}+\ldots=\frac{4 p}{3} .$Similarly $Y$ wins if the outcome is one of the following: $T H, T T T H, T T T T T H, \ldots$
Therefore, the probability that $Y$ wins is

$\frac{1-p}{2}+\frac{1-p}{8}+\frac{1-p}{32}=\frac{2(1-p)}{3}$Since, the probability of winning the game by both the players is equal then, we have

$\frac{4 p}{3}=\frac{2(1-p)}{3} \Rightarrow$p=$\frac{1}{3}$

If two balls are drawn at random, without replacement from a randomly, selected box and one ball turns out to be white while the other ball turns out to be red, then the probability that both balls are drawn from box $B$ is :
questions.solution:
Probability that box $A$ is selected $P\left(A\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Probability that box $B$ is selected $P\left(B\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Let $E$ be the event that one ball is white while the other is red.

$∴ P\left(E\right) = P\left(A\right) \cdot P\left(E / A\right) + P\left(B\right) \cdot P\left(E / B\right)$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{2 \cdot 3}{7{C}_{2}} + \dfrac{4 \cdot 2}{9{C}_{2}}\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{6}{21} + \dfrac{8}{36}\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{2}{7} + \dfrac{2}{9}\right] = \dfrac{16}{63}$

Thus, $P\left(B / E\right) = \dfrac{P\left(B\right)P\left(E / B\right)}{P\left(E\right)} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{9}}{\dfrac{16}{63}} = \dfrac{7}{16}$

questions.q: A bag contains $4$ red and $6$ black balls. A ball is drawn at random from the bag, its color is observed and this ball along with two additional balls of the same color are returned to the bag. If now a ball is drawn at random from the bag, then the probability that this drawn ball is red, is:
questions.solution:
$E:$ Ball drawn from bag is observed to be Red after $A$ or $B$ has occurred.

$P\left(E\right) = P\left(E ∩ A\right) + P\left(E ∩ B\right)$

$⇒ P\left(E\right) = P\left(A\right)P\left(\dfrac{E}{A}\right) + P\left(B\right)P\left(\dfrac{E}{B}\right)$

$= \left(\dfrac{4}{10}\right)\left(\dfrac{6}{12}\right) + \left(\dfrac{6}{10}\right)\left(\dfrac{4}{12}\right)$

$= \dfrac{48}{120}$

$= \dfrac{2}{5}$

questions.q: From a group of $10$ men and $5$ women, four member committees are to be formed each of which must contain at least one women. Then the probability for these committees to have more women than men, is :
questions.solution:
Total number of ways $= C1 5 \times C3 10 + C2 5 \times C2 10 + C3 5 \times C1 10 + C4 5$

$= \dfrac{5 !}{4 !} \times \dfrac{10 !}{7 ! 3 !} + \dfrac{5 !}{2 ! 3 !} \times \dfrac{10 !}{8 ! 2 !} + \dfrac{5 !}{3 ! 2 !} \times \dfrac{10 !}{9 !} + \dfrac{5 !}{4 !}$

$= 5 \times \dfrac{10 \times 9 \times 8}{3 \times 2} + \dfrac{5 \times 4}{2 \times 1} \times \dfrac{10 \times 9}{2} + \dfrac{5 \times 4}{2 \times 1} \times 10 + 5$

$= 5 \times 5 \times 3 \times 8 + 5 \times 2 \times 5 \times 9 + 10 \times 10 + 5$

$= 600 + 450 + 100 + 5 = 1155$

Total no. of ways $= 1155$
No. of ways to form a committee having more women than men
$= 5{c}_{1} \times 10{c}_{{c}_{1}} + 5{c}_{4} = \dfrac{5 !}{3 ! 2 !} \times \dfrac{10 !}{9 !} + \dfrac{5 !}{4 !} = 10 \times 10 + 5 = 105$

probability$= \dfrac{105}{1155} = \dfrac{1}{11}$

questions.q: Let $E \text{ and } F$ be two independent events. The probability that $E \text{ and } F$ happen is $\dfrac{1}{12}$ and the probability that neither $E$ nor $F$ happens is $\dfrac{1}{2}$ , then a value of $\dfrac{P\left(E\right)}{P\left(F\right)}$ is:
questions.solution:
$P\left(E ∩ F\right) = P\left(E\right) . P\left(F\right) = \dfrac{1}{12}$

$⇒ xy = \dfrac{1}{12}$

$⇒ P\left(\overset{-}{E} ∩ \overset{-}{F}\right) = P\left(\overset{-}{E}\right) . P\left(\overset{-}{F}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ \left(1 - P\left(E\right)\right)\left(1 - P\left(F\right)\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ 1 - x - y + xy = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ 1 - x - y + \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ 1 - x - y = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{5}{12}$

$⇒ x + y = \dfrac{7}{12}$

$⇒ x + \dfrac{1}{12x} = \dfrac{7}{12}$

$⇒ ⇒ \dfrac{12{x}^{2} + 1}{12x} = \dfrac{7}{12}$

$⇒ 12{x}^{2} - 7x + 1 = 0$

$⇒ 12{x}^{2} - 4x - 3x + 1 = 0$

$⇒ 4x\left(3x - 1\right) - 1\left(3x - 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{1}{3}, x = \dfrac{1}{4}$

$⇒ y = \dfrac{1}{4}, y = \dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{3}}{\dfrac{1}{4}} \text{ and } \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{4}}{\dfrac{1}{3}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{4}{3} \text{ and } \dfrac{3}{4}$

questions.q: An unbiased coin is tossed eight times. The probability of obtaining at least one head and at least one tail is:
questions.solution:
Probability of at least one head and at least one tail can be calculated as,

$= 1 -{ P\left(AllHead\right) + P\left(AllTail\right) }$

$= 1 - \left\{\dfrac{1}{{2}^{8}} + \dfrac{1}{{2}^{8}}\right\}$

$= 1 - \dfrac{1}{{2}^{7}}$

$= 1 - \dfrac{1}{128} = \dfrac{127}{128}$

questions.q: Three persons P, Q and R independently try to hit a target. If the probabilities of their hitting the target are $\dfrac{3}{4}, \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\dfrac{5}{8}$ respectively, then the probability that the target is hit by P or Q but not by R is:
questions.solution:
Let probability of hitting target by $P$ is ${E}_{1}$ ,$Q$ is ${E}_{2}$ ,and by $R$ is ${E}_{3}$

From the question Required probability is $P ( {E}_{1} ) P ( {E}_{2} ) P ( \overset{¯}{{E}_{3}} ) + P ( \overset{¯}{{E}_{1}} ) P ( {E}_{2} ) P ( \overset{¯}{{E}_{3}} ) + P ( {E}_{1} ) P ( \overset{¯}{{E}_{2}} ) P ( \overset{¯}{{E}_{3}} )$= \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{3}{8}\right) + \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{3}{8}\right) + \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{3}{8}\right)$

$= \dfrac{12 + 9}{64}$

$= \dfrac{21}{64}$

questions.q: If two different numbers are taken from the set $\left\{0, 1, 2, 3, . . . . . , 10\right\}$; then the probability that their sum as well as absolute difference are both multiple of $4$, is:

Required favourable cases are $\left\{\left(0, 4\right), \left(0, 8\right), \left(2, 6\right), \left(2, 10\right)$, $\left(4, 8\right)$, $\left(6, 10\right)$\right\}$

So, favourable cases $= 6$

Total cases ${=}^{11}{C}_{2} = $\dfrac{11 \times 10}{2} =$55$

Hence, the required probability $= $\dfrac{6}{55}

$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: An experiment succeeds twice as often as it fails. The probability of at least $5$ successes in the six trials of this experiment is
questions.solution:
Let $p$ be the probability of successes and $q$ be the probability of failure.

$p = 2q$ and $p + q = 1$

gives $p = \dfrac{2}{3}$ and $q = \dfrac{1}{3}$

For having at least $5$ successes in $6$ trials,

Required probability$= C5 6 {\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}^{5}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + C6 6 {\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}^{6}$

$= C1 6 {\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}^{5}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + C0 6 {\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}^{6}$

$= \dfrac{{6.2}^{5} + 64}{{3}^{6}} = \dfrac{256}{729}$

questions.q: If $A$ and $B$ are any two events such that $P\left(A\right) = \dfrac{2}{5}$ and $P\left(A ∩ B\right) = \dfrac{3}{20},$ then the conditional probability, $P\left(A\left({A}^{′} ∪ {B}^{′}\right)\right),$ where ${A}^{'}$ denotes the complement of $A$, is equal to :
questions.solution:
Given $P\left(A\right) = \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{8}{20}$ & $P\left(A ∩ B\right) = \dfrac{3}{20}$

$∴ P\left({A}^{'} ∪ {B}^{'}\right) = P{\left(A ∩ B\right)}^{'}$

$= 1 - P\left(A ∩ B\right)$

$= 1 - \dfrac{3}{20} = \dfrac{17}{20}$

$P\left(A ∩ \left({A}^{'} ∪ {B}^{'}\right)\right) = P\left(A ∩ {B}^{'}\right)$

$= P\left(A\right) - P\left(A ∩ B\right)$

$= \dfrac{8}{20} - \dfrac{3}{20} = \dfrac{5}{20}$

$∴ P\left(A\left({A}^{'} ∪ {B}^{'}\right)\right) = \dfrac{P\left(A ∩ \left({A}^{'} ∪ {B}^{'}\right)\right)}{P\left({A}^{'} ∪ {B}^{'}\right)}$

$= \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{5}{20}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{17}{20}\right)} = \dfrac{5}{17}$

questions.q:
Let $A$ and $E$ be any two events with positive probabilities

Statement I: $P\left(E / A\right) \ge P\left(A / E\right)P\left(E\right) .$

Statement II: $P\left(A / E\right) \ge P\left(A ∩ E\right) .$
options: Statement - I is false, Statement - II is true
Statement - I is true, Statement - II is false
questions.solution:
We know that $P\left(E / A\right) = \dfrac{P\left(E ∩ A\right)}{P\left(A\right)}$

$⇒ P\left(E ∩ A\right) = P\left(E / A\right) \cdot P\left(A\right) . . . \left(i\right)$

Also, $P\left(A / E\right) = \dfrac{P\left(E ∩ A\right)}{P\left(E\right)}$

$⇒ P\left(E ∩ A\right) = P\left(A / E\right) \cdot P\left(E\right)\left(ii\right)$

From the equations $\left(i\right) and \left(ii\right),$ we get

$P\left(E / A\right) \cdot P\left(A\right) = P\left(A / E\right) \cdot P\left(E\right)$

Now, since $0 < P\left(A\right) \le 1$

$⇒ P\left(E / A\right) \ge P\left(A / E\right) \cdot P\left(E\right)$

Again, we have $P\left(A / E\right) = \dfrac{P\left(E ∩ A\right)}{P\left(E\right)}$

$⇒ P\left(A / E\right) \cdot P\left(E\right) = P\left(E ∩ A\right)$

Now, since $0 < P\left(E\right) \le 1$

$P\left(A / E\right) \ge P\left(A ∩ E\right)$

$⇒$Both the statements are true.

questions.solution:
$P\left(A ∪ B\right) = P\left(A ∩ B\right)$

Using the addition theorem of probability,

$P\left(A ∪ B\right) = P\left(A\right) + P\left(B\right) - P\left(A ∩ B\right)$

$⇒ P\left(A\right) = P\left(B\right)$

Therefore, $P\left(A\right) + P\left(B\right) \ne 1$

Since events A and B are mutually exclusive

questions.q: The probability of a man hitting a target is $\frac{2}{5}$. He fires at the target $k$ times $(k$, a given number). Then the minimum $k$, so that the probability of hitting the target at least once is more than $\frac{7}{10}$, is :
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{2}{5}+\frac{3}{5} \times \frac{2}{5}+\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^$2 $\times \frac{2}{5}+\ldots \ldots+\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^$k $\cdot \frac{2}{5}$>$\frac{7}{10}$\\
\Rightarrow & $\frac{2}{5}\left[$1+$\frac{3}{5}+\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^$2+\ldots \ldots+$\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^$k\right]>$\frac{7}{10}$\\
\Rightarrow & $\frac{2}{5} \times \frac{1-\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^k}{1-\frac{3}{5}}$>$\frac{7}{10} \Rightarrow$1-$\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^$k>$\frac{7}{10}$\\
\Rightarrow & $\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^$k < $\frac{3}{10} \Rightarrow$k \geq 3
\end{aligned}

Hence minimum value$ of k=3$

$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{2}{5}+\frac{3}{5} \times \frac{2}{5}+\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^2 \times \frac{2}{5}+\ldots \ldots+\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^k \cdot \frac{2}{5}>\frac{7}{10} \\
\Rightarrow & \frac{2}{5}\left[1+\frac{3}{5}+\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^2+\ldots \ldots+\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^k\right]>\frac{7}{10} \\

\Rightarrow & \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^k < \frac{3}{10} \Rightarrow k \geq 3
\end{aligned}
$
Hence minimum value of $k=3$

questions.q: If six students, including two particular students $A$ and $B$, stand in a row, then the probability that $A$ and $B$ are separated with one student in between them is
questions.solution:
Consider a group of three students $A, B$ and an other student in between $A$ and $B$. Choice for a student between $A$ and $B$ is 4. $A$ and $B$ can interchange their places in the group in 2 ways.
Now the group of three students (student $A$, student $B$ and a student in between $A$ and $B$ ) and the remaining 3 students can be stand in a row in 4 ! ways.
Hence total number of ways to stand in a row such that $A$ and $B$ are separated with one student in between them $=4 \times 2 \times 4$ !
Now total number of ways to stand 6 student stand in a row without any restriction $=6 !$
Hence required probability

=$\frac{4 \times 2 \times 4 !}{6 !}=\frac{4 \times 2}{6 \times 5}=\frac{4}{15}$

questions.solution:
$\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n i}=\frac{\frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6}}{\frac{n(n+1)}{2}}=\frac{2 n+1}{3}$ For $n=1,2,3, \ldots . ., 1000$ Value of $\frac{2 n+1}{3}=\frac{3}{3}, \frac{5}{3}, \frac{7}{3}, \ldots \ldots \ldots, \frac{2001}{3}$ respectively. Out of $\frac{3}{3}, \frac{5}{3}, \frac{7}{3}, \ldots \ldots \ldots, \frac{2001}{3}$ only first term $\left(\frac{3}{3}=1\right)$, fourth term $\left(\frac{9}{3}=3\right), 667^{\text{th }}$ term $\left(\frac{2001}{3}=667\right)$ are integers.
Hence, out of 1000 values of $\frac{2 n+1}{3}$, total number of integral values of $\frac{2 n+1}{3} =333+1=334 \therefore \quad$ Required probability =$\frac{334}{1000}=$0.334

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $A$ and $B$ be two events such that $P(\overline{A \cup B})=\frac{1}{6}, P(A \cap B)=\frac{1}{4}$ and $P(\bar{A})=\frac{1}{4}$, where $\bar{A}$ stands for complement of event $A$. Then events $A$ and $B$ are
options:
equally likely and mutually exclusive

equally likely but not independent

independent but not equally likely

mutually exclusive and independent
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}$& P(\overline{A \cup B})=$\frac{1}{6},$P(A \cap B)=$\frac{1}{4} \text{$ and }P(\bar{A})=$\frac{1}{4}$\\
& \Rightarrow P(A \cup B)=5 / 6 P(A)=3 / 4 \\
& $\text{ Also }$P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B) \\
& \Rightarrow P(B)=5 / 6-3 / 4+1 / 4=1 / 3 \\
& P(A) P(B)=3 / 4-1 / 3=1 / 4=P(A \cap B)
\end{aligned}

Hence $A and B$ are independent but not equally likely.

$\mathrm{E}_1$ : event denoting that $A$ speaks truth
